solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Beginning to feel the pinch? Mix the double gin with minimal tonic

indicators.note: to mix things is to stir them together, so the letters that follow get jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
gin written twice, since a double is two measures

indicators.note: the smallest possible amount of a word is just its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of tonic

explanation.surface: Someone feeling the pinch stretches a drink: a double gin with barely any tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of THE, GIN, GIN and T are mixed to give TIGHTENING.
explanation.definitionFit: When money gets tight, belts are tightened, and a person starting to feel financial pressure is tightening their spending.

clue.text: Prime Minister in general led by headless power unit

indicators.note: without a head means the word loses its opening letter
in a down clue, to be led by something is to have it come first, on top

parts.note: the watt is the SI unit of power
Robert E. Lee, the Confederate general

explanation.surface: A prime minister is described in general terms, following some beheaded electrical device.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'led by' puts the second part on top, so the power unit comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee was the Labour leader who served as Britain's Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951.

clue.text: At a discount, requiring less than 60% of capital

indicators.note: sixty per cent of a five-letter word is its first three letters, so the last two are dropped

parts.note: below means less than
Paris is the capital of France

explanation.surface: A bargain purchase that needs less than sixty per cent of the money invested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like money in this financial surface, but it is a capital city: three fifths of PARIS is PAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A share trading below its nominal or face value is said to be at a discount to it.

clue.text: Bar bishop knocking out rector in protest

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop

indicators.note: knocking something out removes it, so one letter is taken away

parts.note: to rail against something is to protest about it
R is an abbreviation for rector

explanation.surface: At a protest, a bishop knocks out a rector in a brawl at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: B joins RAIL, and then the R for rector is knocked out to leave B + AIL.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a bail is one of the two small wooden crosspieces resting on top of the stumps, a little bar.

clue.text: Dictator's wise to constrain festival failing to exhibit a notice in the past

indicators.note: to constrain is to hold in, so one part wraps round the other
a dictator here is someone dictating aloud, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: said aloud, wise is the same as Ys, two of the letter Y

indicators.note: a word that fails to show the letter a has had that letter taken out

parts.note: Easter is a Christian festival
to give ear is to take notice

explanation.surface: A dictator's sage decision to curb a festival that won't put up a notice, a thing of the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' here is someone dictating, so 'wise' is heard as the letter name Ys, giving a pair of Ys that bracket the festival.
explanation.definitionFit: Yesteryear can be used adverbially to mean during former times, in days gone by.

clue.text: Weird fringes of party supporting tribe

indicators.note: in a down entry, a part that supports another sits underneath it

parts.note: the Cree are a Native American people

indicators.note: the fringes of a word are its edges, its first and last letters

parts.note: the outside letters of party

explanation.surface: Odd figures on the edge of a political party who back a tribal group.
explanation.definitionFit: Something creepy is strange and unsettling, giving an uneasy feeling of the uncanny.

clue.text: Drivers' club run by night probed by very nosy individual

indicators.note: something probed has another thing pushed inside it

parts.note: the AA is the Automobile Association, the British motoring organisation
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
night-time is the dark
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A motoring club out at night is investigated by a very nosy person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very nosy' reads as one phrase, but 'very' is wordplay and only 'nosy individual' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The aardvark has a long snout for rooting out termites, so it is literally a nosy creature.

clue.text: Some people start to terrify with call for attention

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of terrify
hey is a shout to catch someone's notice

explanation.surface: Some people begin frightening others by shouting to be noticed.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun they refers to an unspecified group, as in 'they say it will rain'.

clue.text: Naughty Seth and Marnie bathe together

indicators.note: naughty means misbehaving, so the letters will not stay in their proper places

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two people misbehaving by taking a bath together.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of SETH, MARNIE and BATHE are rearranged; 'and' only joins the two names.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying two things in the same breath means saying them at the same moment, simultaneously.

clue.text: Hottest spot gets lowest score? That's unexpected

parts.note: hell is traditionally the hottest place there is
zero, the lowest score, looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A sweltering venue earns the lowest marks, a surprising verdict.
explanation.definitionFit: Hello can be an exclamation of surprise, as in 'hello, what's going on here?'

clue.text: Already set up to adopt Times Modern

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so one part is placed inside the other
something set up has been arranged anew, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time, so times plural is two of them

explanation.surface: Someone already arranged to take on a newspaper, The Times, with modern ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper; it is two Ts, which go inside the rearranged ALREADY.
explanation.definitionFit: Latter-day means belonging to recent times, a present-day version of something older.

clue.text: Organ introit's a revelation

parts.note: the eye is an organ of sight
an introit is the opening chant of a church service

explanation.surface: The opening voluntary on the church organ proves a revelation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ' suggests a church instrument to go with the introit, but it is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye-opener is something surprising or enlightening that shows the truth of a matter.

clue.text: Routine sort of job in spinning setter's keeping clear of

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so these outer parts enclose another
spinning round turns the short word to face the other way

parts.note: taken as written
the setter says I have, shortened to I've
net of means after deductions, as clear of tax

explanation.surface: A routine job is described in terms of a setter going round in circles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter's' means the setter has, I've; net of is accounting language for after deductions.
explanation.definitionFit: A nine-to-five job keeps regular office hours, the standard working day of a salaried employee.

clue.text: I agree to curb extremely abstract poet

indicators.note: to curb is to restrain, holding something in

parts.note: yes is what you say to agree

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, the first and last letters

parts.note: the end letters of abstract

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to rein in a poet whose work is far too abstract.
explanation.definitionFit: W. B. Yeats was the Irish poet who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923.

clue.text: Mineral water in London park inadequately described

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a green rock-forming mineral with a snakeskin pattern
second meaning: the lake in Hyde Park, which the setter admits is described only loosely

explanation.surface: Mineral water in a London park, poorly labelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mineral water' reads as one bottled drink, but the two words belong to separate meanings; 'inadequately described' is the setter's wry admission that a park lake is a thin clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Serpentine is a mottled green magnesium silicate rock, and the Serpentine is the recreational lake in Hyde Park.

clue.text: Agent on commission transformed Runcorn bakeries

indicators.note: a thing transformed has changed its form, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: taken as written; Runcorn is a town in Cheshire
taken as written

explanation.surface: A commissioned agent has given the bakeries of Runcorn a makeover.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurance broker arranges cover for clients and is paid commission by the insurers on each policy sold.

clue.text: Mushroom cocktail

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb, to grow rapidly in size
second meaning: a drink of advocaat and lemonade

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mushroom' looks like a noun, a fungus garnish for a cocktail, but it is the verb meaning to expand fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A rolling snowball grows bigger as it gathers snow, and the Snowball is a popular British Christmas drink.

clue.text: Dolores is to run rings around anyone standing up to her

indicators.note: the words ring around, forming a circle that encloses what is sought

parts.note: concealed across the end of Dolores, the next two words and the start of run

explanation.surface: Dolores easily outdoes anyone who dares to oppose her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run rings around' is an idiom for outclassing, but here 'run' is part of the hidden letters and 'rings around' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A resistor is one who resists, someone who opposes and refuses to give way.

clue.text: Total loss or guaranteed returns (not much)?

indicators.note: something that returns comes back the way it went
only a small part of the phrase is wanted, a few letters from within it

parts.note: the letters straddling the end of loss, all of or and the start of guaranteed

explanation.surface: An investor weighs a total loss against meagre but guaranteed returns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns' looks like investment income; it says to read the hidden letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A gross figure is the whole amount before deductions, the total.

clue.text: Polish assembly once cloaked in silence

indicators.note: something cloaked is wrapped up inside a covering

parts.note: sh is the hush call for silence
a moot was an Anglo-Saxon public assembly

explanation.surface: A Polish parliament of the past holds its sessions in silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' is capitalised to suggest Poland; it is the verb meaning to buff to a shine.
explanation.definitionFit: Buffing a surface removes roughness and leaves it sleek and even, so the verb is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Winger converts first of tries against Spain

parts.note: to convert something is to turn it into something else

indicators.note: the first of a word is just its initial letter

parts.note: the opening letter of tries
on means against, as in leaning on the wall
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: A rugby wing converts the first of his side's tries in the match against Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby a winger scores tries and a conversion follows, but here 'Winger' means a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The turnstone is a small wading bird that flips over pebbles to find food; any bird is a winged creature.

clue.text: Manx cat the French officer raised as a wild animal

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something turns it upside down so it reads bottom to top
Manx cats are born without tails, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
le is French for the
CO is a commanding officer

explanation.surface: A tailless cat that a French officer brought up has turned out to be a wild beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manx cat' seems a single item, but Manx tells you to dock TOM to TO; TO + LE + CO then reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a spotted wild cat of the Americas, a medium-sized predator of forests.

clue.text: One may rumble an underdog, apparently

definitions.text: One may rumble an underdog, apparently

parts.note: surface reading: someone might see through the weaker contender's bluff
setter's reading: split it as a dog that is under, a low barker, and the deep rumbling loudspeaker emerges

explanation.surface: Someone may find out the plucky outsider's game.
explanation.walkthrough: SUB means under and a WOOFER is a dog, so the word looks like an underdog; it is the speaker for low bass notes, which rumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A subwoofer is a loudspeaker reproducing the lowest bass frequencies, the ones you feel as a rumble.

clue.text: Arrange play without regard to Pinter's introduction

indicators.note: doing without something means leaving it out

parts.note: to sport is to play

indicators.note: the introduction to a name is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the playwright's name

explanation.surface: Staging a play while ignoring the introduction Harold Pinter wrote for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' and 'Pinter' suggest the theatre, but play is SPORT, which loses its P.
explanation.definitionFit: To sort things is to put them in order or classify them, to arrange them.

clue.text: Ready to take two subjects at school

wordplay.note: RI is religious instruction and PE physical education, two British school subjects

explanation.surface: A pupil is ready to take two school subjects as exams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready to take' suggests sitting an exam; it means fit to be picked.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripe fruit is mature enough to be harvested or eaten, ready for picking.

clue.text: Broadcast enchanted Cologne?

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard rather than read, so the word goes by its sound

parts.note: sent can mean thrilled or transported with delight

explanation.surface: A radio programme about the enchanted German city of Cologne.
explanation.walkthrough: Cologne looks like the German city, but the question mark marks it as an example of a perfume.
explanation.definitionFit: Eau de Cologne is a light perfume, so Cologne is one example of a scent.

clue.text: It could be that no pair volunteer to move

indicators.note: letters that move change places, ending in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: It may be that not one couple offers to relocate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It could be that' reads as hedging; it actually means the word that is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Words like that, which, who and whom are grammatical pronouns introducing a subordinate clause.
